title: Algebraic description of complex conjugation on cohomology of a smooth projective hypersurface

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2.3 (last paragraph) / statement of Theorem 2.3
candidates.exact_quote: Then in view of Lemma 2.5, finding \(\phi_{\mathbb{C}}^{-1}(\phi_{\mathbb{C}}(U_k))\) for \(U_k = y^i f_{j_i}(x)\) amounts to finding \(h_{j_i}(x)\) such that \(R(y^i f_{j_i}, y^{n-1-i}h_{j_i}) = U_{k,\gamma}\). Now it is clear that \(h_{j_i} = \tilde{f}_{j_i}\) as defined in (2.10) satisfies the desired condition.
candidates.claim_content: Setup: X is a smooth degree-e hypersurface in P^n defined by G(x), A = k[y,x], S = yG, Jac(S) = (yG_0,...,yG_n,G), c_X = e-(n+1). Griffiths' isomorphism phi_C : A_{c_X}⊗C / (Jac(S)∩(A_{c_X}⊗C)) → H_0 = ⊕_{p+q=n-1} H_0^{p,q} sends the weight-r part (spanned by classes [y^r f(x)], deg f = e(r+1)-(n+1)) isomorphically onto H_0^{n-1-r,r}. Lemma 2.5 states that the transported pairing satisfies R([y^i f],[y^j g]) = b_{i,j}(2π√-1)^{n-1} e(e-1)^n r_{f g} when i+j = n-1 and 0 otherwise, where r_h is the unique scalar with h ≡ r_h · D mod Jac(G) = (G_0,...,G_n) and D = det(∂²G/∂x_i∂x_j). Theorem 2.3 asserts: given U_k = y^i f_{j_i}, choose ANY polynomial y^{n-1-i}g_{j_i} ∈ A_{c_X} with f_{j_i}g_{j_i} ∉ Jac(G); set f̃_{j_i} := [b_{i,n-1-i} U_{k,γ} / (r_{f_{j_i} g_{j_i}} (2π√-1)^{n-1} e (e-1)^n)] · g_{j_i}; then the complex conjugate of phi_C([y^i f_{j_i}]) equals phi_C([y^{n-1-i} f̃_{j_i}]). Claim under scrutiny: the single numerical equation R([y^i f_{j_i}],[y^{n-1-i}h]) = U_{k,γ} determines the class [y^{n-1-i}h] uniquely, so that h = f̃_{j_i} must be the conjugate.
candidates.suspected_defect: The element conj(phi_C(U_k)) ∈ H_0^{i,n-1-i} = phi_C(weight-(n-1-i) part) is determined only by its pairings against ALL of the weight-i part, not by the single pairing against U_k. The equation R(U_k, y^{n-1-i}h) = U_{k,γ} has an affine hyperplane of solutions whenever dim_C H_0^{n-1-i,i} > 1. Indeed the theorem lets g_{j_i} be ARBITRARY subject to f_{j_i}g_{j_i} ∉ Jac(G); replacing g by g + h0 with f_{j_i} h0 ∈ Jac(G) but h0 ∉ Jac(G) (possible as soon as the complementary graded piece of the Jacobian ring has dimension > 1, e.g. plane quintics where dim H^{1,0}=6) leaves the scalar unchanged but changes the resulting class [y^{n-1-i} f̃]. Hence the conclusion cannot hold for all admissible choices, and the proof establishes only one linear condition among the many needed.

candidates.claim_content: Notation: phi_C : A_{c_X}⊗C/(Jac(S)∩(A_{c_X}⊗C)) → H_0 = ⊕_{p+q=n-1}H_0^{p,q} is Griffiths' isomorphism; P is the Hodge-decomposition isomorphism H^{n-1}_prim(X,Q)⊗C ≅ H_0; the conjugation on H_0 is the ANTILINEAR involution induced by 1⊗c, whose fixed set is H^{n-1}_prim(X,R). Theorem 2.3 provides, for each chosen basis element U_j = y^i f_{j_i}, a polynomial f̃_{j_i} with conj(phi_C([y^i f_{j_i}])) = phi_C([y^{n-1-i} f̃_{j_i}]); the paper's footnote asserts the conjugate of [y^{n-1-i}f̃_{j_i}] is [y^i f_{j_i}]. Corollary 2.7 sets w_{j} = (y^i f_{j_i} + y^{n-1-i} f̃_{j_i})/2 and claims (phi_C^{-1}∘P)(H^{n-1}_prim(X,R)) = Σ_j ( R·[w_j] + R·[√-1 · w_j] ).
candidates.suspected_defect: If conj(w) = w (w is fixed by the antilinear conjugation), then conj(√-1 w) = -√-1 conj(w) = -√-1 w, so √-1·w is NOT in the fixed set. The right-hand side Σ_j (R w_j + R √-1 w_j) = ⊕_j C w_j is a COMPLEX subspace, whereas the real form H^{n-1}_prim(X,R) is a totally real subspace of H_0 and is never a complex subspace (for μ>0). The correct second generator should be √-1·u_j with u_j = (y^i f_{j_i} - y^{n-1-i} f̃_{j_i})/2, since conj(u_j) = -u_j gives conj(√-1 u_j) = √-1 u_j. The same error is repeated in Example 2.8 for the elliptic curve, where the real cohomology H^1(X,R) is 2-dimensional over R but is not the complex line C·[(1+μ y D(x))/2].

candidates.error_location: Section 2.4 (odd n), Definition 2.6 / formula for U_{k,γ} with the matrix P
candidates.claim_content: Setting: n = 2m+1 odd, X a smooth hypersurface of dimension 2m in P^n. H_{2m}(X,Z)_0 = ker(H_{2m}(X,Z)→H_{2m}(P^n,Z)) carries a symmetric non-degenerate intersection form whose matrix in a chosen basis γ_1,...,γ_μ is P, with det(γ_α·γ_β) = ±e (so P is NOT unimodular when e>1). The paper's proof identifies H_0 = ⊕H_0^{p,q} with homology via ω ↦ Σ_i (∫_{γ_i}ω)γ_i and asserts that the cup-product pairing C(ω,ω') = ∫_X ω∧ω' equals B(image(ω),image(ω')) = Σ_{i,j} (∫_{γ_i}ω)(γ_i·γ_j)(∫_{γ_j}ω'), i.e. that ∫_X ω∧ω' = Σ_{i,j}(∫_{γ_i}ω) P_{ij} (∫_{γ_j}ω'). Question: is this identity correct with the intersection matrix P itself, or with its inverse?
candidates.suspected_defect: In the dual basis η_i (∫_{γ_i}η_j = δ_{ij}) one has ω = Σ(∫_{γ_i}ω)η_i, and the matrix M_{ij} = ∫_X η_i∧η_j equals the inverse-transpose of the intersection matrix, M = (P^T)^{-1} = P^{-1} (symmetric case). For the even-n case the standard symplectic Q happens to satisfy (Q^T)^{-1} = Q, so the paper's formula is correct there; but for odd n with det P = ±e ≠ ±1 one has P^{-1} ≠ P, so U_{k,γ} and the matrix product P_X·P·conj(P_X)^T should use P^{-1} (equivalently the inverse of the intersection matrix). Concrete test: smooth quadric surface in P^3 (n=3, e=2), primitive H_2 generated by γ with γ·γ = -2; then ∫_X ω∧ω = -(1/2)(∫_γ ω)^2, not -2(∫_γ ω)^2.

candidates.claim_content: For a smooth hypersurface X ⊂ P^n of degree e, the paper states μ = dim_C H^{n-1}_prim(X,C) = \frac{e-1}{e}\left((e-1)^n + (-1)^{n+1}\right), and then asserts that e>1 implies μ>0 (and, for n = 2m+2 even, that μ = 2g with g a positive integer).
candidates.suspected_defect: For e = 2 and n even the formula gives μ = (1/2)(1^n + (-1)^{n+1}) = (1/2)(1-1) = 0. E.g. a smooth conic in P^2 (n=2,e=2) has b_1 = 0, and a quadric threefold in P^4 (n=4,e=2) has b_3 = 0. So 'e>1 implies μ>0' is false, and the subsequent assertion that μ = 2g with g a positive integer fails in these cases.

candidates.error_location: Subsection 2.1, relative long exact sequence and tubular neighborhood isomorphism
candidates.exact_quote:
$$
\cdots \longrightarrow H_{n-1}(\mathbb{P}^n, \mathbb{P}^n \setminus X) \longrightarrow H_n(\mathbb{P}^n \setminus X) \longrightarrow H_n(\mathbb{P}^n) \longrightarrow H_n(\mathbb{P}^n, \mathbb{P}^n \setminus X) \longrightarrow \cdots
$$
candidates.claim_content: X ⊂ P^n is a smooth hypersurface (complex codimension 1, real codimension 2). The paper writes the long exact homology sequence of the pair (P^n, P^n∖X) beginning with the arrow H_{n-1}(P^n,P^n∖X) → H_n(P^n∖X), and then asserts the isomorphism H_{n-1}(P^n, P^n∖X) ≅ H_{n-1}(X) 'using a tubular neighborhood of X in P^n', from which the tube map T : H_{n-1}(X,C) → H_n(P^n∖X,C) is obtained.
candidates.suspected_defect: The connecting map in the long exact sequence of a pair goes H_k(P^n,P^n∖X) → H_{k-1}(P^n∖X); to land in H_n(P^n∖X) the source must be H_{n+1}(P^n,P^n∖X), not H_{n-1}(P^n,P^n∖X). Correspondingly the Thom/tubular-neighborhood isomorphism for a real-codimension-2 submanifold reads H_k(P^n, P^n∖X) ≅ H_{k-2}(X), so H_{n+1}(P^n,P^n∖X) ≅ H_{n-1}(X), not H_{n-1}(P^n,P^n∖X) ≅ H_{n-1}(X). Both indices are off by 2.

candidates.exact_quote: ∑_{j ∈ I₀ ⊔···⊔ Iₘ} (ℝ·[wⱼ] + ℝ·[√−1 wⱼ])    if |Iₘ| is even
candidates.claim_content: For n = 2m+1 odd, μ = dim_C H^{n-1}_prim(X,C) = Σ_{q=0}^{2m}|I_q| where |I_q| = dim_C H_0^{n-1-q,q} and Hodge symmetry gives |I_q| = |I_{2m-q}|. The basis chosen in (2.18) is {y^i f_{j_i} : i=0,...,m-1, j_i = 1,...,|I_i|} ∪ {y^m f_{j_m} : j_m = 1,...,⌈|I_m|/2⌉}. Corollary 2.7 claims (phi_C^{-1}∘P)(H^{n-1}_prim(X,R)) = Σ_{j ∈ I_0⊔···⊔I_m}(R[w_j] + R[√-1 w_j]) when |I_m| is even, and Σ_{j ∈ I_0⊔···⊔I_m∖{α}}(R[w_j]+R[√-1 w_j]) + R[w_α] when |I_m| is odd, where α = ⌈|I_m|/2⌉ ∈ I_m.
candidates.suspected_defect: Dimension count: H^{n-1}_prim(X,R) has real dimension μ = 2Σ_{q<m}|I_q| + |I_m|. But the index set written, j ranging over ALL of I_0⊔···⊔I_m, gives 2(Σ_{q<m}|I_q| + |I_m|) = μ + |I_m| real dimensions in the even-|I_m| case, and 2(Σ_{q<m}|I_q|+|I_m|-1)+1 = μ + |I_m| - 1 in the odd case. These exceed μ unless |I_m| = 0 (resp. 1). The index set should be restricted to the ⌈|I_m|/2⌉ elements of I_m used in (2.18).

candidates.claim_content: For n = 2m+1, the paper selects a set of classes {U_1,...,U_a} = {y^i f_{j_i} : i = 0,...,m-1, j_i = 1,...,|I_i|} ∪ {y^m f_{j_m} : j_m = 1,...,⌊|I_m| + 1/2⌋}, where |I_q| = dim_C H_0^{n-1-q,q}, and forms an a × μ period matrix from them. For the subsequent dimension bookkeeping (half of the total μ = 2Σ_{q<m}|I_q| + |I_m|, rounded up) one needs a = Σ_{q<m}|I_q| + ⌈|I_m|/2⌉.
candidates.suspected_defect: As written, ⌊|I_m| + 1/2⌋ = |I_m| for any integer |I_m|, which gives too many elements (a = Σ_{q≤m}|I_q| > μ/2 in general) and makes the chosen classes exceed 'half' of the cohomology. The intended quantity is ⌈|I_m|/2⌉ = ⌊(|I_m|+1)/2⌋.

candidates.claim_content: For a smooth plane cubic (n = 2, e = 3) with canonical basis γ_1,γ_2 of H_1(X,Z) (intersection matrix Q = [[0,1],[-1,0]]) and ω = phi_C([1]), the quantity appearing in Theorem 2.3 is U_{1,γ} = Σ_{i,j}∫_{γ_i}ω (γ_i·γ_j) conj(∫_{γ_j}ω) = ∫_{γ_1}ω · conj(∫_{γ_2}ω) − ∫_{γ_2}ω · conj(∫_{γ_1}ω), and the scalar in (2.10) is U_{1,γ}/((2π√-1)^{n-1} e (e-1)^n) = U_{1,γ}/(2π√-1 · 3 · 4) = U_{1,γ}/(24π√-1) (with b_{0,1} = (-1)^{0+1+1} = +1).
candidates.suspected_defect: As printed, the numerator ∫_{γ_1}ω·∫_{γ_2}ω − ∫_{γ_2}ω·∫_{γ_1}ω is identically zero (the complex conjugation bars on the second factors are missing), so the displayed μ is 0, which would make the claimed conjugate class vanish. Worth checking that the intended numerator carries the conjugates, and that the constant 24π√-1 = (2π√-1)e(e-1)^n for n=2,e=3 is correct.

candidates.exact_quote: one can think of an element of H^1_B(E_σ, Q) ≅ H^1(C/Z^2, Q) as of the form Qdx + Qdy, where z = x + iy is a coordinate for C
candidates.claim_content: E is an elliptic curve over Q with the real embedding σ: Q ↪ R ⊂ C; E_σ(C) ≅ C/Λ for a lattice Λ. The paper identifies E_σ(C) with C/Z^2 and asserts that H^1_B(E_σ,Q) = Q dx + Q dy where z = x + iy, and that ι_σ(dx) = dx, ι_σ(dy) = -dy.
candidates.suspected_defect: A general elliptic curve over Q with a real embedding has period lattice Λ = Z ω_1 + Z ω_2 which is not Z + Zi; identifying E_σ(C) with C/Z^2 is a genuine restriction. More importantly, the real 1-forms dx and dy need not be rational cohomology classes: for Λ = Z·1 + Z·τ with τ = (1+it)/2 and t irrational, ∫_τ dy = t/2 ∉ Q, so dy ∉ H^1(E,Q). Hence 'H^1_B(E_σ,Q) = Q dx + Q dy' is false in general; only the real/complex statements hold.

candidates.error_location: Equation (2.16) and the Grothendieck residue normalisation
candidates.exact_quote: \int_{\mathbb{P}^n}\left[\frac{h(x)\Omega_x}{\frac{\partial G}{\partial x_0} \frac{\partial G}{\partial x_1} \ldots \frac{\partial G}{\partial x_n}}\right] = \frac{(2\pi\sqrt{-1})^n}{e-1}\operatorname{Res}_0 \left\{\frac{h(x)}{\frac{\partial G}{\partial x_0} \cdots \frac{\partial G}{\partial x_n}}\right\}
candidates.claim_content: G is a homogeneous polynomial of degree e in x_0,...,x_n defining a smooth hypersurface X ⊂ P^n; Ω_x = Σ_i (-1)^i x_i dx_0∧···∧\widehat{dx_i}∧···∧dx_n; h is homogeneous of degree (n+1)(e-2); D = det(∂²G/∂x_i∂x_j); r_h is defined by h ≡ r_h D mod (G_0,...,G_n). The paper asserts (i) ∫_{P^n}[hΩ_x/(∂G/∂x_0 ··· ∂G/∂x_n)] = (2π√-1)^n/(e-1) · Res_0{h/(∂G/∂x_0···∂G/∂x_n)}, (ii) Res_0{h/(∂G/∂x_0···∂G/∂x_n)} = (e-1)^{n+1} r_h, and hence (2.16): ∫_{P^n}[...] = (2π√-1)^n (e-1)^n r_h.
candidates.suspected_defect: The factor 1/(e-1) in (i) is not derived in the paper and the normalisation of the trace map ∫_{P^n} on H^n(P^n,Ω^n) versus the local Grothendieck residue at the origin of C^{n+1} is delicate; the combination of (i) and (ii) feeds directly into the constant b_{i,j}(2π√-1)^{n-1}e(e-1)^n r_{fg} of Lemma 2.5 and hence into the main formula (2.10). Worth independent checking (e.g. with G = x_0^e + ... + x_n^e, or the case n=1, e=2 where D = 4 and Res_0 = h/4).

candidates.claim_content: For i + j = n-1 and homogeneous A, B with deg A = e(i+1)-(n+1), deg B = e(j+1)-(n+1), the paper quotes from Carlson–Griffiths: δ( res(AΩ_x/G^{i+1}) · res(BΩ_x/G^{j+1}) ) = c_{i,j} · A B Ω_x/(∂G/∂x_0 ··· ∂G/∂x_n) with c_{i,j} = (-1)^{i(i+1)/2 + j(j+1)/2 + n-1 + j^2} e /(i! j!), and defines b_{i,j} = (-1)^{i(i+1)/2 + j(j+1)/2 + j^2}. In the proof of Lemma 2.5 they use c_{i,j}(-1)^{i+j} i! j! = b_{i,j} e.
candidates.suspected_defect: The exponent and the factor e in c_{i,j} are taken verbatim from a cited source and are not derived; any error here propagates directly into Lemma 2.5's pairing formula R([y^i f],[y^j g]) = b_{i,j}(2π√-1)^{n-1}e(e-1)^n r_{fg} and into the main formula (2.10). Internal consistency c_{i,j}(-1)^{n-1}i!j! = b_{i,j}e holds, but the absolute constant (including the factor e and the sign exponent j^2 + n-1) should be verified independently.
